entries.signature: SELECT [TOP n] [DISTINCT] <fields> FROM <source> [JOIN ...] [WHERE ...] [GROUP BY ... [HAVING ...]] [ORDER BY ...] [TOTALS ... BY ...] [UNION ...]  ·  YEAR/MONTH/DAY(...) · BEGINOFPERIOD/ENDOFPERIOD(...) · DATEADD/DATEDIFF(...) · SUBSTRING(...) · <expr> REFS <Kind>.<Name>
entries.description:
The query language reads configuration data declaratively: you name metaobjects and attributes, the platform builds the SQL for the connected DBMS itself.

**How a query is written.** The query text is a plain string. Sources are named by metaobject kind and name: `Catalog.Products`, `Document.Expense`, `InformationRegister.Prices`, plus register virtual tables (`AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&Period)`). Attributes are named directly, including reference dereference through a dot: `Item.Producer.Description` — the platform builds the joins itself. Values travel as `&Name` parameters. Keywords are case-insensitive.

**How a query executes.** `New Query(text)` parses the text once (one parse — many executions). On `Execute()`:
1. the optimizer simplifies the query tree (normalizes NOT, flattens simple subqueries into one SELECT);
2. names resolve against the metadata and the query lowers onto the universal read door;
3. providers execute it: physical tables run as ONE SQL statement in the DBMS (joins and aggregations go server-side whenever possible); computed sources (slices, balances, aggregate subqueries) are computed by the engine and stitched with physical data when needed; on PostgreSQL large intermediates materialize into DB temporary tables so the join still runs server-side.

The result is a `QueryResult`; traversal goes through `QuerySelect` (a flat cursor or a totals tree — one and the same interface).

**Access.** User-authored query text is read-only (SELECT); data changes go through the object model. If the user's role carries a row-level restriction (RLS), it folds into the query at the same read door — a query cannot escape it (see "Row-level security (RLS) — overview").

See the "Data queries" category for per-clause articles.

The query object. The constructor parses the text immediately (syntax errors surface right away, with line and position); the parsed tree is cached, so one object can execute many times with different parameters.

**Methods:**
- `SetParameter(name, value)` — set the value of an `&name` parameter (without the ampersand). Names are case-insensitive. An unset parameter is an execution error.
- `Execute()` — run and return a `QueryResult`. Every call re-reads the data.
entries.parameters: text — the query text (see "Query language — overview").

entries.description:
The result of executing a query — a single data snapshot. Detail rows and totals read from the same snapshot, so they cannot diverge.

**Methods:**
- `Select()` — open a traversal. For a plain SELECT it returns a flat cursor; for a TOTALS query — the totals tree. Both come back as a `QuerySelect` with one and the same traversal interface.
entries.syntax_block:
var res = q.Execute();
var sel = res.Select();

entries.description:
The selection — a cursor over the result rows. Result columns read as properties named after the output column (the attribute name or the `AS` alias).

**Methods and properties:**
- `Next()` — advance to the next row; false at the end.
- `Reset()` — rewind to the start.
- `<ColumnName>` — the column value of the current row (references come back as objects, so you can navigate further).
- `Level()` — node depth (totals tree; 0 = root).
- `HasChildren()` — whether nested nodes exist.
- `Select()` — descend into the current node's children: returns a nested QuerySelect (recursive traversal of the totals tree).
- `Total(name)` — the grand total of a column (over the whole result).

In a TOTALS query an aggregated column reads as the level subtotal on a group node and as the row value on a leaf.
entries.syntax_block:
var sel = res.Select();
while (sel.Next()) { ... sel.Price ... }

entries.description:
The output list.

- `*` — every attribute of the source (with a JOIN — of all sources).
- A field — an attribute name, optionally prefixed by the source alias (`t.Code`) and dereferenced through dots (`Item.Producer.Description`).
- An **expression** — arithmetic (`Price * Quantity`) and `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END`; read back by alias. Single source.
- An **aggregate** — `SUM / MIN / MAX / AVG (field | dereference | expression)`, `COUNT(* | field)`; makes the query a grouping one (see GROUP BY).
- `AS alias` (or a bare identifier after the field) — the output name; the selection reads the column by it.
- `TOP n` — at most n result rows. In a union: the FIRST branch's TOP caps the WHOLE union, a later branch's TOP caps that branch; in a subquery — the subquery rows. Works with GROUP BY too (caps the groups); not combinable with TOTALS.
- `DISTINCT` — no duplicate rows.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT TOP 10 DISTINCT Producer.Region AS Region,
       Price * Quantity AS Amount,
       CASE WHEN Quantity > 100 THEN "bulk" ELSE "unit" END AS Kind
FROM Document.Sale

entries.description:
The data source.

**Metaobjects:** `Catalog.X`, `Document.X`, `Enumeration.X`, `InformationRegister.X`, `AccumulationRegister.X`, `AccountingRegister.X`, `Constant.X`, `ChartOfAccounts.X`, `ChartOfCharacteristicTypes.X`; tabular sections — `Document.X.Goods`. Reports and data processors are not query sources.

**Register virtual tables** — a third name segment, arguments in parentheses (values and parameters):
- `InformationRegister.Prices.SliceLast(&Period [, &Filter])` / `.SliceFirst(...)` — the latest/earliest slice;
- `AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&Period [, &Filter])` — balances;
- `AccumulationRegister.Stock.Turnovers(&From, &To [, &Filter])` — turnovers.
No arguments = as of now / no filter.

**Subquery:** `FROM (SELECT ...) AS s` — a nested SELECT as a source, including an **aggregate** one (`SELECT Cat, SUM(x) AS s ... GROUP BY Cat`): the outer query sees the group keys and the aggregate aliases, and an outer condition on an aggregate alias behaves like HAVING. Simple subqueries are flattened into one SELECT by the optimizer automatically.

The source alias prefixes field names (`t.Code`).
entries.syntax_block:
FROM AccumulationRegister.WarehouseStock.Balance(&AsOf) AS bal
FROM (SELECT Producer, SUM(Weight) AS W FROM Catalog.Products GROUP BY Producer) AS s
entries.example:
// balances as of a date, filtered outside
SELECT Item, QuantityBalance
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&Period)
WHERE QuantityBalance > 0

entries.signature: [INNER | LEFT | RIGHT | FULL [OUTER]] JOIN <source> [AS alias] [ON <condition> | ON TRUE]
entries.description:
A horizontal join of sources.

- Kinds: `INNER` (the default for a bare JOIN), `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`; the word `OUTER` is optional.
- `ON a.x = b.y` — a key equality (operand order is free). This is the fast path: a hash join, pushed down to the server whenever possible.
- `ON a.x <op> b.y` — an **inequality** (`<> < <= > >=`), a theta join. It runs as a nested-loop over pairs in engine memory — expensive on large sets, unlike the equality path.
- `ON a.x + 1 = b.y` — a **computed** condition (an expression on either side): also a nested-loop over pairs; there are no key columns here.
- `ON b.x <op> value / &param` — a **constant** condition (a `value(...)`, `&parameter`, or literal on one side): by SQL this is a cross join filtered on that column, so it is emitted as such — INNER joins only (for an outer join put the condition in WHERE).
- `ON TRUE` — the cartesian product (cross join).
- No `ON` — auto-join by reference: when a field of one source references the other, the key derives automatically.

With a JOIN, project columns explicitly (by aliases); `SELECT *` expands every source. Two physical tables join in ONE server-side SQL statement; a computed side (a slice, balances, a subquery) materializes into a DBMS temporary table when large enough (PostgreSQL), else the engine stitches it; pure-inner chains of three or more sources are re-joined smallest-first by their real sizes.

**Current limits:** a boolean WHERE (OR/NOT/IN/IS NULL) with a JOIN works when the join runs as one SQL statement; dot-walk in WHERE/GROUP BY with a JOIN is not supported yet (in the projection — supported on a single source).
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT p.Description, b.QuantityBalance
FROM Catalog.Products AS p
LEFT JOIN AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&P) AS b ON p.Ref = b.Item

WHERE (Price > &Min OR Producer.Region = &Reg)
  AND Description LIKE "A%"
  AND Posted = TRUE

entries.description:
Flat grouping: one result row per group.

- Group keys are fields or dereferences (`GROUP BY Producer.Region`); every non-aggregate output must be a key.
- Aggregates in the projection: `SUM / MIN / MAX / AVG (field | dereference | expression)`, `COUNT(*)`. An expression input (`SUM(Price * Quantity)`) needs a single physical source.
- A COMPUTED output beside the aggregates is a group key of its own: `ISNULL(QuantityBalance, 0) AS Rest`, `CASE WHEN … END AS Kind`. Anything built from keys is one — what it may NOT be built from is an aggregate's result (`ISNULL(SUM(Qty), 0)`), which exists only after the fold. Fold a computed input instead: `SUM(Price * Quantity)`.
- `HAVING` filters the groups after aggregation; conditions combine with `AND` (write as many as you need), operators `= <> < <= > >=`.
- WHERE or HAVING is not a decision you have to make. A condition over an aggregate is a group filter wherever it was written, and a condition over a group key is a row filter wherever it was written — the engine puts each where it runs. Both give the same answer: a key cannot vary inside its group.
- `TOP n` caps the number of groups.

Grouping by a reference field uses reference IDENTITY (two distinct items with the same description do not merge).

On a single physical source the grouping runs in the DBMS; over a computed source (a slice, a subquery) the engine folds it. HAVING over a computed source is not supported yet (an outer condition on an aggregate subquery is).
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT Producer.Region AS Region, SUM(Weight) AS Weight, COUNT(*) AS Items
FROM Catalog.Products
GROUP BY Producer.Region
HAVING SUM(Weight) > 100

entries.description:
Result ordering. Ascending by default (`ASC`); `DESC` descends. A dereference is allowed (`ORDER BY Producer.Description`).

Besides a field you can order by an **expression** — arithmetic or `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... END` ("sort by a condition"), and by a bare constant (`&parameter` / `value(...)`). An expression order runs on a single physical source. A plain field / dereference sort can page a large result incrementally; an expression sort reads the ordered result whole.

In a union, ORDER BY is written once at the end and sorts the whole result (by the first branch's column names).
entries.syntax_block:
ORDER BY CASE WHEN Priority = &High THEN 0 ELSE 1 END,
         Producer.Description, Price DESC

entries.name_local: Query package (INTO / ONTO / DROP, temporary tables)
entries.name_en: Query package (INTO / ONTO / DROP, temporary tables)
entries.description:
Several statements in ONE query text, separated by `;`. Each statement sees the temporary tables the ones before it made — that is what a package is for.

- `INTO <TempTable>` — put this result into a temporary table instead of returning it. Later statements read it by the bare name: `FROM Folded AS f`.
- `ONTO <Name>` — NAME the result this statement returns, so it can be asked for by name instead of by position.
- **Both are written right after the SELECT list, BEFORE `FROM`** — `SELECT Goods, SUM(Qty) AS Qty INTO Folded FROM …`. They are mutually exclusive: INTO returns no result, so there would be nothing to name.
- `INDEX BY <field>{, …}` — index the temporary table this statement makes (only with INTO); written after the query body.
- `DROP <TempTable>` — release it early. A statement of its own, and it returns nothing.

**Reading the results** (`Query` methods):
- `ExecuteBatch()` — an **Array** of results, indexed by the position each statement was written at. An INTO statement answers with one row holding the record count; a DROP answers Undefined.
- `Execute()` — the FIRST result, which for an ordinary one-statement query is the only one.
- `LINK <Name>` — the result a statement named with ONTO.

**Living longer than one execution:** without a `TempTablesManager` the tables die with the call that made them. Attach one to both queries and they are shared: `manager = New TempTablesManager(); first.TempTablesManager = manager; … second.TempTablesManager = manager; … manager.Close();`.

A package runs as ONE trip and inside one read state, so every statement sees the same data.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT M.Goods AS Goods, SUM(M.Quantity) AS Qty
INTO Folded
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock AS M
GROUP BY M.Goods
INDEX BY Goods;

SELECT G.Description AS Item, f.Qty AS Qty
FROM Catalog.Products AS G
INNER JOIN Folded AS f ON f.Goods = G.Ref;

DROP Folded

entries.description:
Hierarchical totals: the result is a TREE with a subtotal at every level and the grand total at the root (unlike the flat GROUP BY).

- Aggregates between `TOTALS` and `BY` (`SUM(Quantity)`, `COUNT(*)`, a computed measure named by a SELECT alias — `SELECT 1 AS pcs ... TOTALS SUM(pcs)`) roll IN-PLACE: a group node reads the subtotal off the same column a leaf reads the row value from.
- **Aggregates are optional:** `TOTALS BY Warehouse` is a pure grouping into a tree with no rolled measure (this is how a grouped list is built). If `BY` follows `TOTALS` immediately, there are no aggregates.
- Dimensions after `BY` apply IN ORDER — each is a tree level. A scalar dereference is allowed (`BY Parent.Code`) — the platform auto-joins the reference path.
- `HIERARCHY` unfolds a reference dimension along its catalog's hierarchy (folders become nodes); `HIERARCHYONLY` keeps only the hierarchy nodes — a leaf element is not emitted as its own row but still counts towards the totals; `ELEMENTS` (the default) — by values.

**Sources.** Works on a single source, with a `JOIN` (it shares the source-tree build with the ordinary read path), and with a `UNION`: the branches stack vertically and the dimensions / aggregates resolve against the **first** branch's columns — like the trailing ORDER BY of a plain union.

Reading: `res.Select()` returns the tree — `Level()`, `HasChildren()`, descend via `Select()`, the grand total via `Total(name)` (see QuerySelect). Detail and totals fold from ONE snapshot — they cannot diverge.

**Limits:** a dereferenced dimension takes a scalar leaf; TOP does not combine with TOTALS; inside a subquery or a UNION branch `TOTALS` (like `JOIN`) is not allowed yet — write them at the top level.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT Warehouse, Item, Quantity
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&P)
TOTALS SUM(Quantity) BY Warehouse, Item HIERARCHY

// no aggregate — just a tree by a dimension
SELECT Description, Price FROM Catalog.Products
TOTALS BY Producer

entries.description:
Vertical stacking of results. Branch columns match BY NAME of the output columns; a column missing in a branch yields an empty value.

- `UNION` — removes duplicates from the accumulated result at that operator (equivalent to a distinct over the stack).
- `UNION ALL` — keeps duplicates.
- Semantics are left-associative: `A UNION B UNION ALL C` dedupes after B, keeps C's duplicates.
- The trailing ORDER BY applies to the whole union. The first branch's TOP caps the whole result; a later branch's TOP caps that branch.

A union of physical tables runs as one server-side SQL statement (native UNION / UNION ALL); computed branches go to DB temporary tables when large enough (PostgreSQL) or are stacked by the engine.

**Limits:** branches may not use JOIN or TOTALS yet.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT Code, Description FROM Catalog.Products
UNION ALL
SELECT Code, Description FROM Catalog.Services
ORDER BY Description

entries.description:
Parameters pass values into a query safely: text is never concatenated with data, values reach the DBMS as bound parameters — injection is impossible by construction.

- In the text — `&Name` anywhere a value is allowed: comparisons, IN, BETWEEN, virtual-table arguments (`Balance(&Period, &Filter)`).
- Set with `q.SetParameter("Name", value)` before `Execute()`; names are case-insensitive; an unset parameter is an execution error.
- Value types: number, string, date, boolean, reference (obtain a reference via the object model or a subquery).

Always pass dates as parameters — the language has no date literals.

A literal reference written straight in the query text — the empty reference of a metaobject, or one of its predefined items — so you need not pass it as a parameter.

- `value(Catalog.Currencies.EmptyRef)` — the EMPTY reference of that catalog (a typed empty, not NULL).
- `value(Catalog.Accounts.Cash)` — the reference to a PREDEFINED item by name (catalogs and charts of accounts / characteristic types carry predefined items).
- `EmptyRef` is case-insensitive; a predefined name matches as defined. An unknown metaobject or member is a query error (with the position).

**Where it works:** anywhere a value is expected — a comparison / IN / BETWEEN right side, a JOIN ON, the projection (`SELECT value(...) AS x`), inside a CASE. It behaves exactly like a bound parameter, only the value is resolved from the metadata instead of `SetParameter`.
entries.syntax_block:
WHERE Account  = value(ChartOfAccounts.Main.Cash)
  AND Partner <> value(Catalog.Partners.EmptyRef)
entries.example:
// tag each union branch with a predefined catalog item
SELECT Ref, value(Catalog.DocKinds.Incoming) AS Kind FROM Document.Receipt
UNION ALL
SELECT Ref, value(Catalog.DocKinds.Outgoing) AS Kind FROM Document.Expense

entries.description:
A dot after a reference field reads an attribute of the referenced object; the platform builds the necessary joins automatically (a LEFT JOIN on the reference key). Chains can be any length: `Item.Producer.Region.Description`.

**Where it works:** the projection, WHERE (including boolean combinations, IN, IS NULL), ORDER BY, GROUP BY, aggregate inputs, TOTALS BY dimensions (scalar leaf). Single source; paths sharing a prefix share one join.

**Empty and broken references** do not drop the row: the attribute reads as the TYPED EMPTY of its type (not NULL) — matching the object model.

**Composite references** (a field referencing several types — e.g. a register's Recorder): the platform joins only the types that actually carry the requested attribute and takes the matching branch's value. This also works for a REFERENCE attribute behind a composite segment (`Recorder.Partner`). Filtering / sorting by such a reference attribute behind a composite segment is not supported yet (a scalar one is).
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT Description, Producer.Region.Description AS Region
FROM Catalog.Products
WHERE Producer.Region = &Reg
ORDER BY Producer.Description
entries.example:
// a composite reference: the attribute exists on a few recorder types only
SELECT Recorder.Partner AS Who, SUM(Quantity) AS Q
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock
GROUP BY Recorder.Partner

entries.name_local: Date parts — YEAR, MONTH, DAY and the rest
entries.name_en: Date parts — YEAR, MONTH, DAY and the rest
entries.signature: YEAR(<date>) | QUARTER(<date>) | MONTH(<date>) | DAYOFYEAR(<date>) | DAY(<date>) | WEEK(<date>) | WEEKDAY(<date>) | HOUR(<date>) | MINUTE(<date>) | SECOND(<date>)
entries.description:
One piece of a date, as a NUMBER. Ten calls of one shape: the argument is any date expression — a field, a &parameter, another calendar call — and the answer is an ordinary number to group by, compare and total.

- `WEEKDAY` is **Monday = 1 … Sunday = 7** (ISO), the same on every DBMS: the platform pins the numbering rather than passing the engine's own through, so a report reads alike wherever it runs.
- `WEEK` is the ISO week of the year; `DAYOFYEAR` counts from 1; `SECOND` answers whole seconds.

**These are not keywords.** `YEAR`, `MONTH`, `DAY` and the rest stay available as ATTRIBUTE names — a call is recognised by the bracket after it, so a catalog with a `Year` attribute keeps reading it.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT
	YEAR(Doc.Date) AS Y,
	MONTH(Doc.Date) AS M,
	WEEKDAY(Doc.Date) AS Weekday
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
WHERE YEAR(Doc.Date) = 2026
entries.example:
// how much left the warehouse per weekday
SELECT WEEKDAY(M.Period) AS Weekday, SUM(M.Quantity) AS Qty
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock AS M
GROUP BY WEEKDAY(M.Period)

entries.description:
The first and the last moment of the period a date falls in. The period is one of: Second, Minute, Hour, Day, Week, Month, Quarter, HalfYear, Year — the same words a register's virtual table takes for its periodicity, because it is the same vocabulary.

- `ENDOFPERIOD` answers the LAST instant the period still covers (one second before the next begins), so `BETWEEN BEGINOFPERIOD(&D, Month) AND ENDOFPERIOD(&D, Month)` covers the whole month with nothing falling between two comparisons.
- The date may be a &parameter, a field, or another call — `BEGINOFPERIOD(&AsOf, Quarter)` is the ordinary way to say "since the quarter began".
- `TenDays` is refused here: the last ten-day bucket of a month runs 8 to 11 days, so it is a bucket rather than a length and nothing can be moved by it.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT
	BEGINOFPERIOD(Doc.Date, Month) AS MonthStart,
	ENDOFPERIOD(Doc.Date, Month) AS MonthEnd
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
entries.example:
// everything written this quarter
SELECT Doc.Ref AS Doc
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
WHERE Doc.Date BETWEEN BEGINOFPERIOD(&AsOf, Quarter) AND ENDOFPERIOD(&AsOf, Quarter)

entries.name_local: DATEADD — move a date by whole periods
entries.name_en: DATEADD — move a date by whole periods
entries.description:
Move a date by whole periods — Second, Minute, Hour, Day, Week, Month, Quarter, HalfYear, Year. The count may be negative, which is how "a month ago" is written.

It is CALENDAR arithmetic, not a number of days: adding a month to the 31st lands on the last day of a shorter month, which is what a person means by "a month later" and what adding 30 days gets wrong. The same answer is computed in memory when a reading cannot be pushed to the server, so a query does not change its mind about dates depending on how it ran.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT
	DATEADD(Doc.Date, Day, 30) AS DueDate,
	DATEADD(Doc.Date, Month, -1) AS MonthBefore
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
entries.example:
// invoices past their thirty days
SELECT Doc.Ref AS Doc
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
WHERE DATEADD(Doc.Date, Day, 30) < &Today

entries.name_local: DATEDIFF — whole periods between two dates
entries.name_en: DATEDIFF — whole periods between two dates
entries.description:
How many WHOLE periods lie between two dates — Second, Minute, Hour, Day, Week, Month, Quarter, HalfYear, Year. Negative when the second is earlier.

Whole periods means BOUNDARIES CROSSED, not a span divided by a length: from the 31st of January to the 1st of February is one month, because they are different months, and two moments of one day are zero days apart.

This is the call a "how long did it hold" reading is built out of: pair each row with the next one and take the difference between their dates.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT DATEDIFF(Doc.Date, &Today, Day) AS DaysOld
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
entries.example:
// how long each price held
SELECT P.Period AS Since,
	DATEDIFF(P.Period, ISNULL(MIN(N.Period), &Till), Day) AS Days
FROM InformationRegister.Prices AS P
	LEFT JOIN InformationRegister.Prices AS N
		ON N.Item = P.Item AND N.Period > P.Period
GROUP BY P.Item, P.Period

entries.name_local: DATETIME — a date written as its parts
entries.name_en: DATETIME — a date written as its parts
entries.description:
A date CONSTANT, written as numbers instead of a literal. Every argument has to be a constant — a number or a &parameter — because the value is settled once, before the query runs, and travels as the date it denotes.

Give it a field and it is refused, with that as the reason: a date built per row out of columns is a different thing and this is not it.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT Doc.Ref AS Doc
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
WHERE Doc.Date >= DATETIME(2026, 1, 1)
entries.example:
SELECT Doc.Ref AS Doc
FROM Document.Expense AS Doc
WHERE Doc.Date BETWEEN DATETIME(2026, 1, 1) AND DATETIME(2026, 3, 31, 23, 59, 59)

entries.description:
Part of a string, counted FROM ONE: `SUBSTRING(Code, 1, 3)` is the first three characters. A `from` past the end, or a length of zero, answers with an empty string rather than failing.

The same answer is computed in memory when the reading cannot be pushed to the server, so the two roads agree.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT SUBSTRING(G.Code, 1, 3) AS Prefix, G.Description AS Item
FROM Catalog.Goods AS G
entries.example:
// how many items per code prefix
SELECT SUBSTRING(G.Code, 1, 3) AS Prefix, COUNT(*) AS Items
FROM Catalog.Goods AS G
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(G.Code, 1, 3)

entries.name_local: REFS / VALUETYPE / TYPE — which type is in this row
entries.name_en: REFS / VALUETYPE / TYPE — which type is in this row
entries.description:
A composite field — a register's recorder, a document's basis, a characteristic's value — may hold a reference to any of several tables. These ask WHICH one is in this row.

- `Basis REFS Document.Expense` — a predicate, true when the field points at that table.
- `VALUETYPE(Basis) = TYPE(Document.Expense)` is the same question in the other spelling, and the engine reads it as the same thing.
- `NOT REFS` (or `<>` on the second form) negates it.

**It is a TEST, not a narrowing.** It answers yes or no and reads nothing out of the target. To WALK into the type — `CAST(Recorder AS Document.Expense).Number` — use CAST, which says which type is meant and continues the dot from there. The two are written together often: test in the WHERE, walk in the selection.

A field that cannot hold a reference at all (a number, a string) answers FALSE rather than failing — "it does not point there" is a complete answer.
entries.syntax_block:
SELECT M.Recorder AS Doc, M.Quantity AS Qty
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock AS M
WHERE M.Recorder REFS Document.Expense
entries.example:
// the number of the document behind each movement of one kind
SELECT
	CAST(M.Recorder AS Document.Expense).Number AS ExpenseNo,
	M.Quantity AS Qty
FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock AS M
WHERE VALUETYPE(M.Recorder) = TYPE(Document.Expense)
